title: Measuring {{term:angle}}s with a {{term:protractor}}
summary: Read and draw angles with a protractor. Find angles on a straight line, vertically opposite angles and angle bisectors.
guide: A {{term:protractor}} is a half circle split into 180 equal parts. Each part is one {{term:degree-angle}} (1°).
To read an angle: put the centre of the protractor on the vertex and its zero line along one arm. Then read the number where the other arm crosses.
A protractor has two scales. Read the scale that starts at 0 on your first arm. An acute angle is less than 90°; an obtuse angle is more than 90°.
Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Two angles that add up to 180° are {{term:supplementary-angles}}.
When two lines cross, {{term:vertically-opposite-angles}} are equal.
An {{term:angle-bisector}} cuts an angle into two equal angles.
Turn the protractor with your finger, or tap it and use the arrow keys. Near an arm it snaps into place.

engine.label-arm: Arm of the angle; drag to turn it

read-angle.title: How big is this angle?
read-angle.prompt: First estimate: is this angle acute or obtuse? Now turn the protractor until its zero line lies along one arm. How many degrees is the angle?
read-angle.hint: Turn the protractor until its straight edge sits on the lower arm. Count from the 0 on that arm and see which number the other arm reaches.
read-angle.success: Well done! The angle is 65°. It is acute, so it had to be less than 90°.
read-angle.why: The protractor has two scales. How did you know which one to read?
read-angle.model: I read the scale that is 0 on the first arm. The angle is acute, so the answer is less than 90°: 65°, not 115°. 65 + 115 = 180.

feedback.other-scale: You read the other scale. The angle is acute, so it must be less than 90°.
feedback.not-from-zero: The protractor's zero line is not on an arm of the angle. Turn the protractor until it sits on one arm first.
feedback.not-aligned: Your number is right, but measure it with the protractor: turn it until its zero line lies on an arm.
feedback.too-big: Your number is too big. Count again from 0.
feedback.too-small: Your number is too small. Count again from 0.

draw-angle.title: Draw a 130° angle
draw-angle.prompt: Turn the coloured arm until it makes an angle of 130° with the lower arm. First think: is 130° acute or obtuse?
draw-angle.hint: 130 is more than 90, so the angle is obtuse. Count from the 0 on the right: 90, 100, 110, 120, 130.
draw-angle.success: Well done! A 130° angle is obtuse.
draw-angle.why: How did you make sure you used the right scale?
draw-angle.model: The lower arm points right, and the outer scale is 0 on the right, so I counted on the outer scale. 130 is more than 90, so the angle must be obtuse, and it is.

feedback.other-scale: That is a 50° angle: you used the other scale. A 130° angle must be obtuse.
feedback.too-big: The angle is too big. Turn the arm back a little.
feedback.too-small: The angle is too small. Turn the arm further.

angle-on-line.title: Angles on a straight line
angle-on-line.prompt: On a straight line, the small angle is 70°. How big is the marked angle? No protractor this time. Reason it out!
angle-on-line.hint: A straight line makes a straight angle: 180°. The two angles on the line add up to 180°.
angle-on-line.why: Why do two angles next to each other on a straight line add up to 180°?
angle-on-line.model: A straight line covers a whole half turn, like the straight edge of a protractor from 0 to 180. Together the two angles fill that half turn, so 70 + 110 = 180.

feedback.same: The marked angle is obtuse, so it is not 70°. The two angles add up to 180°.
feedback.used-90: 90° is a right angle. On a straight line the angles add up to 180°.
feedback.used-360: 360° is a full turn round a point. On a straight line the angles add up to 180°.
feedback.too-big: Your number is too big. The two angles must add up to 180°.
feedback.too-small: Your number is too small. The two angles must add up to 180°.

vertically-opposite.title: Vertically opposite angles
vertically-opposite.prompt: Two lines cross. The top angle is 125°. How big is the bottom angle? Predict first, then check with the protractor.
vertically-opposite.hint: The angle at the side is on a straight line with the 125°, so it is 55°. The bottom angle is on a straight line with that same 55°.
vertically-opposite.success: Well done! The bottom angle is 125° too. Vertically opposite angles are equal.
vertically-opposite.why: Why are vertically opposite angles equal?
vertically-opposite.model: The side angle is on a straight line with both of them. So 125 + 55 = 180, and bottom + 55 = 180. Both make 180 with the same 55°, so they are equal: 125°.

feedback.adjacent: 55° is the angle at the side. Find the opposite one, at the bottom.
feedback.other-scale: You read the other scale. The bottom angle is obtuse, so it is more than 90°.
feedback.too-big: Your number is too big. Compare the bottom angle with the top one.
feedback.too-small: Your number is too small. Compare the bottom angle with the top one.

bisect.title: Bisect the angle
bisect.prompt: This angle is 100°. Turn the coloured arm until it cuts the angle into two equal halves.
bisect.hint: What is half of 100? Put the arm on that number.
bisect.success: Well done! The coloured arm is at 50°. 50 + 50 = 100. It is the angle bisector.
bisect.why: How do you know the coloured arm cuts the angle in half?
bisect.model: The angle between the lower arm and the coloured arm is 50°. The angle between the coloured arm and the other arm is 100 − 50 = 50°. The two angles are equal, so the coloured arm is the bisector.

feedback.whole: The coloured arm is on top of the other arm. The bisector must be in the middle of the angle.
feedback.right-angle: That is a right angle. The middle of 100° is not 90°. Work out half of 100.
feedback.too-big: The arm has gone past the middle. Turn it back a little.
feedback.too-small: The arm has not reached the middle yet. Turn it further.
